label: Shot size
description: Shot sizes, from an extreme close-up to an extreme wide shot. Most are named for how much of a person they show (head and shoulders, waist up, knees up, full length); close-ups, detail shots and wide shots suit any subject.
notes: Shot sizes belong here, from extreme close-up through extreme wide, phrased as named shots with an article. The subject facet marks the crops named by a person's body (head and shoulders, waist up, knees up) apart from sizes that suit any subject. Chest-up and medium close-up share one entry; three-quarter shot means a knee-up crop here, while cowboy shot ends at mid-thigh. camera.angle owns viewpoints (profile, over the shoulder, point of view); camera.selfie owns selfies; camera.genre owns group portraits and two-shots; camera.composition owns negative space, frames within the frame and reflections; camera.lens owns lenses and camera.film_look owns film and formats.

values.look: A tiny feature, such as one eye or a mouth, fills the frame; the rest of the subject is cut off.
The face or main subject fills nearly the entire frame, with little background visible.
One small part of a larger subject fills the image, such as stitching on a coat or a carved door handle.
The entire head and the tops of both shoulders show, with the crop near the collarbone.
The head, shoulders, and upper chest show; the frame ends around the middle of the chest.
The person is framed from the waist up, leaving room for arms, hands, and some background.
The person is framed from the head to mid-thigh, keeping the hips and hands beside them visible.
Only the body between the neck and waist is visible; the head and legs fall outside the frame.
The person is visible from the head to around the knees, with the lower legs and feet outside the frame.
The entire person is visible from head to feet and occupies most of the frame height.
The whole subject is visible with ample space around it, making the surrounding setting easy to read.
A broad view identifies the location, showing a building or landscape together with its immediate surroundings.
The setting dominates the image; any person is a tiny figure within a much larger landscape or space.
